words.etymon: *gʷem- (present βαίνω < *gʷm̥-yé-; the perfect stem βεβη- is built on *gʷeh₂-)

cognate: *sóh₂wl̥ (sūra-/sūrya- ~ ἠέλιος) + *médʰyo- (madhya- ~ μέσος), with the perfect-system form of the 'go/step' verb (Ved. jagāma, MBh gata- to gam; Gk ἀμφιβεβήκει to βαίνω)
drift_or_renewal: the 'sky/path' noun is renewed: Ved. adhvan- 'road' (AV), div- (RV madhye divaḥ) vs Gk οὐρανός; the Greek perfect stem βεβη- is rebuilt on *gʷeh₂- inside the βαίνω paradigm, so the verb forms are same-lexeme rather than strict formal cognates
shared_syntax: sun as subject + perfect (pluperfect) of the go-verb + 'middle (of sky/road)' as accusative of goal/extent (AV vi madhyam; Il. μέσον οὐρανὸν); MBh has the same three elements as a locative absolute (madhya-gate sūrye)
context: a time-of-day marker, 'when the sun had reached the middle (of its course)', at a turning point of the action: in Il. 8.68 (also 16.777) it introduces Zeus' weighing of fates at noon in the battle; in MBh 7.70 it times a battle; in AV 7.72 it marks the moment of the midday offering to Indra
phrase: 'the sun has gone to the middle (of heaven/its road)': Ved. jagāma sūro adhvano vi madhyam ~ Hom. Ἠέλιος μέσον οὐρανὸν ἀμφιβεβήκει ~ Ep. Skt. madhya-gate sūrye
note: Low: noon described by the sun in mid-sky is close to universal and the words are each language's default for sun and middle, so the cognates count for little. What makes it worth recording is the shared verb (the go-verb in a perfect form) and the matching aspect, in a timing formula. The ON pivot 'midur daghur ... skijn sol' (Þiðreks saga, translated from German) is only the generic midday and is not part of the claim. 'Recalled' refers to the Il. 16.777 repetition and to the formal history of βέβηκα.

near_miss.lead: night + dark of *mergʷ-: ON 'myrkt var af nott' / 'nott er myrk' ~ Serbian 'мрклој ноћи мрака'
near_miss.why_not: Searched: 'myrkt (var/gerði) af nótt' is a fixed Old Norse saga prose phrase (Egils, Grettis, Finnboga, Jómsvíkinga, Þiðreks saga, Heimskringla), and Serbian мрк-/мрак goes with night but also, much more often, with wine, moustaches, wolves and horses ('мрко вино', 'мрки брци'). The *mergʷ- root is shared by Germanic and Slavic only, I found no Old English or Eddic 'mirce/myrk + night', and 'dark night' is the default collocation in any language. It is a shared word, not a shared phrase.

near_miss.lead: ON 'watn ath drekka edur bygg eta' ~ Hitt. 'wātar akuwanzi ... adanzi' (*wódr̥ + *h₁ed-, eat/drink merism; ON bygg 'barley', and the Kikkuli horses are fed barley too)
near_miss.why_not: Eat-and-drink and drink-water are universal. The Hittite is a horse-training manual and the ON is an old king's lament ('thirsted and hungered', 'barley bread and water', with biblical colouring). The drink verbs differ (drekka vs eku-). I do not see a formula here.

near_miss.lead: ON 'hefur hannz nafn ... aukest myked vid þessa frægd' (his name increased greatly) ~ *h₁nómn̥ + *h₂ewg-
near_miss.why_not: MBh 'nāmataḥ karmatas' is about name and deed, not name-growing. Searching *h₁nómn̥ + *h₂ewg- finds only ON 'jók nafn hans' (biblical, Gen. 12:2) and grammatical texts. The figure is Christian or generic.

near_miss.lead: ON 'med hinum mesta blóma' ~ Lat. 'aetatis ... florem' (*bʰleh₃- 'flower' as prime/splendour)
near_miss.why_not: The ON is 'with the greatest splendour/honour' (court hospitality), a translated romance and probably a calque of MLG blôme. Lucretius means youth's prime. The contexts differ and the metaphor is widespread in medieval Europe.

near_miss.lead: father + son + *priHós (ON fader ... frændur; AV pitā putram iva priyam)
near_miss.why_not: In the ON the father lists kinsmen (frændr), while the AV has the simile 'as a father (clothes) his dear son'. No common syntax or figure.

near_miss.lead: *lewbʰ- 'praise/love' with son: ON 'Gud see þess lofadur ... þinn son' ~ ORu. 'сн҃ъ мои възлюбленыи'
near_miss.why_not: Both are Christian formulae (ON doxology, ORu. quotation of Matt. 3:17). The ON lofa is 'praise', not 'love', and is not tied to the son.

near_miss.lead: dogs fed with flesh (*ḱwṓ): ON 'gefa sinumm hundumm' ~ Il. 'κύνας κεφαλῆς'
near_miss.why_not: The ON is the hunt's reward to the hounds. The Iliad is the threat that dogs will devour an unburied enemy. Different motif and no shared wording beyond 'dog'.

near_miss.lead: 'dog' as insult/epithet: ON 'sa hinn ille hunndur Attila' ~ Irish cú
near_miss.why_not: The Irish cú here is a heroic kenning (or an OCR form), not an insult, and in the Revue Celtique passage 'coin' is not 'dog' (see error line). Dog as a term of abuse is universal.

near_miss.lead: ON 'klyfur hialminn og hofudid' (cleaves helmet and head to the teeth) ~ Cato 'capita ... interficis'
near_miss.why_not: The ON is a chivalric stock blow from the German-derived romance. Cato means 'heads' = persons. No congruence.

near_miss.lead: size + strength of a hero/giant (ON 'afl er sua mikit'; Hdt. 'μέγαθος ... ἰσχύν'; Svyatogor turning the earth)
near_miss.why_not: The words for strength are not cognate (afl / ἰσχύς / bylina has none) and the motif is generic.

near_miss.lead: shining like stars + gold (ON 'hialmur glóar sem fimm stiørnur ... sem gull' ~ Av. 'tištrīm stārəm ... zarańiiō')
near_miss.why_not: The ON is a simile for armour in a translated romance. The Avestan is an invocation of the star Tištriia with a golden-horned bull's form. Star and gold co-occur everywhere.

near_miss.lead: glory dies with the man (ON 'er egh er daudur þa er ok daud oll vár tign')
near_miss.why_not: No partner in the bundle continues it (Herodotus, Thucydides and MBh are unrelated), and the ON is a translated romance whose sentiment is the opposite of the Eddic 'orðstírr deyr aldregi'. No phrase is shared.

error.correct_reading: cona (co 'with' + 3sg fem. possessive a): 'co ndeachaid Erne cona hingenaib' = 'Erne went with her maidens'
error.evidence: The h-prefixed hingenaib (dat. pl. of ingen) needs a preceding fem. possessive a. The Loch Erne story has Erne and her maidens drowning in the lake, which the passage goes on to say.

error.correct_reading: hríð f. 'a while' in 'langa hríd' (a long while)
error.evidence: Context 'berriast ... langa hríd til þess er myrkt var' = they fought a long while until it was dark. It has nothing to do with *wreyt- 'twist'.

error.correct_reading: proper name Gunnarr, should be unmapped
error.evidence: Personal name (King Gunnarr), mapped through its second element.

error.correct_reading: Κάλης (river name, acc. Κάλητα), proper name
error.evidence: 'ἐς τὸν Κάλητα ποταμὸν'. The lemma 'ξαλες' is garbled.

error.correct_reading: ethnic name Ἴωνες (dat. pl.), should be unmapped
error.evidence: It is a proper ethnic name and has no connection with *yos.

note: Second reader of 17 flagged bundles only. One low-confidence claim (sun gone to mid-heaven, BS-a62a6), 12 near-miss lines (the three dark-night bundles in one line) and 5 error lines.
